theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A school in May Pen asks for "new security grills for the classrooms". Before planning, what should Andre, the team leader, do first?
options: Order the steel at once so that it is ready on time
Start making grills to the size of the last job
Agree the exact scope: windows, sizes, design, finish and date
Send a price based on a guess of the number of windows

questions.stem: What is the "scope of work" in a job plan?
options: The total price the customer will pay
The list of tools kept in the workshop
The names of the people on the team
What will and will not be done on the job

questions.stem: The customer's sketch and the written specification disagree about the finish. What should the planner do?
options: Pick the cheaper finish to keep the price down
Follow the sketch, as drawings always win
Query it and get the answer in writing
Use whichever finish the team likes best

questions.stem: Why does a Level 3 planner visit the site before planning a gate installation at a house in Mandeville?
options: To confirm sizes, access, power and hazards the drawing may not show
To meet the neighbours and tell them about the work
To count how many windows the house has in total
To find a place to park the van on the day

questions.stem: Which job objective is clear enough to plan from?
options: Make some nice railings for the stairs soon
Do the best job possible on the stair railing
Finish the railings some time when the team has some free time
Fit 12 m of painted stair railing to drawing R2 by 15 March

questions.stem: What is a work breakdown structure (WBS)?
options: A chart of who reports to whom in the company
A record of breakdowns on each workshop machine
A list of all the faults found at the final inspection of the job
The job split into smaller tasks that can be planned

questions.stem: The primer on a gate must dry for 24 hours before the topcoat is put on. How is this wait best shown in the plan?
options: As a lag (wait) between the two tasks
As a task that can be skipped if late
As extra work for the welders to do
As time the painters must stand by the job and watch it

questions.stem: Which order of work is best for making and fitting balcony rails at a guest house in Port Antonio?
options: Paint, cut, weld, measure on site, fit
Cut, weld, paint, then measure on site, fit
Measure on site, cut, fit, paint, weld
Measure on site, cut, weld, paint, fit

questions.stem: A frame job has three tasks: cut the parts (4 h), weld the frame (6 h) and make the brackets (3 h). The brackets can be made by a second welder while the frame is welded. What is the shortest time to finish?
options: 13 hours
7 hours
10 hours
9 hours

questions.stem: What is the critical path in a job plan?
options: The chain of tasks that sets the shortest finish time
The route the forklift takes through the workshop
The tasks that carry the greatest safety risk on the job
The list of tasks that the customer must pay for first

questions.stem: A task on the critical path runs one day late. If nothing else changes, what happens to the finish date?
options: It stays the same, because the other tasks will catch up
The whole job will finish one day later
It moves earlier, because the team will work faster
Only that one task's end date changes

questions.stem: What is "float" (slack) on a task?
options: The extra steel bought in case of waste
How long a task can slip without delaying the job
The time the paint needs to dry before handling
The money kept aside for unexpected problems at the end

questions.stem: Task A takes 3 days and Task B takes 5 days. Both start on day 1, and both must finish before Task C can start. How much float does Task A have?
options: 5 days
3 days
8 days
2 days

questions.stem: What is a milestone in a job plan?
options: A key point, such as "frame passed"
A task that takes longer than one full week
The heaviest item that the team must lift
A stone marker placed at the edge of the site

questions.stem: Why should the bar chart (schedule) for a long job be updated each week?
options: So that it looks neat when the customer visits
Because the chart fades if it is not redrawn
So progress, delays and the new finish date can be seen
So the team can change the order of tasks without telling anyone

questions.stem: A job needs 96 welder-hours. Three welders each work 8 hours a day. How many days will the welding take?
options: 4 days
12 days
8 days
32 days

questions.stem: Why should the plan check that the right machines will be free on the days they are needed?
options: Because machines run better when they are booked early
So that every machine is used every day of the week
Another job may be using them, which would hold up this one
So the team can choose a different job if they are busy

questions.stem: For which job is it most important to name a qualified (certified) welder in the plan?
options: Tack welding a practice piece at the Centre
Welds on a pressure pipe to a code
Spot welding a sheet metal tray for a shop
Grinding the edges of a practice plate

questions.stem: The plan needs two welders on Monday, four on Tuesday and two again on Wednesday. What is the best fix?
options: Hire two extra welders for Tuesday only, at any cost
Ask the welders to work twice as fast on Tuesday
Leave it, as the numbers even out over the week
Use float to move tasks and level out the labour

questions.stem: Why does a planner find out how long each material will take to arrive before setting the start date?
options: Some items take weeks to arrive, which would hold up the job
So that the steel can be stored outside for longer
So the supplier can charge a higher price for speed
Because steel bought early will always be cheaper

questions.stem: A frame needs 46 m of square tube. Tube comes in 6 m lengths, and the planner adds 10% for waste. How many lengths should be ordered?
options: 8 lengths
10 lengths
7 lengths
9 lengths

questions.stem: Why does a planner group the cut list by material size before ordering?
options: So that each piece is cut by a different person
So stock lengths can be shared and waste kept low
So the pieces are welded in alphabetical order
So that the supplier delivers each size on a different day

questions.stem: Why does a Level 3 planner add a contingency allowance of time or money to a job estimate?
options: To cover risks that may happen, such as rain or late delivery
To make more profit without telling the customer
So the team can take longer breaks on the job
Because every estimate must be doubled to be safe

questions.stem: Labour is costed at J$1 800 per hour. A job needs 35 hours. What is the labour cost?
An estimate is J$250 000 before GCT. Why should the plan show GCT as a separate line, worked out at the current rate?
options: Because GCT is the same rate on every item forever
So the planner can choose whether to charge it
The rate may change, and it must be clear
Because GCT is only charged on labour, not parts

questions.stem: A job plan includes welding inside a water tank. Which extra planning step is needed?
options: Weld faster so the welder spends less time inside
A permit to enter, gas testing and a standby person
Use a smaller electrode so that less fume is produced
Open the tank lid and start work as soon as possible, to save time

questions.stem: Some galvanised steel must be welded. Which control should the plan put first?
options: Wear a paper dust mask while welding the parts
Weld it outside on a windy day to blow the fume
Work quickly so the welder breathes less fume
Grind off the zinc and use extraction

questions.stem: Before hot work on a client's site, who usually issues the hot work permit?
options: Any welder in the team who is free that day
The supplier who delivered the gas cylinders
The person in charge of the site, or the client's safety officer
The customer's neighbour, if the work is near their fence line

questions.stem: Why should the plan for a site job list the emergency arrangements, such as first aid and the nearest hospital?
options: So help comes fast if someone is hurt
Because the customer pays extra for the list
So that the team can visit the hospital on the way
Only because the form has a box for it to fill

questions.stem: The plan has a crane lift of a 400 kg gate over a public footpath in Spanish Town. Which extra step is most needed?
options: Ask people walking by to move quickly
Do the lift at night with no lights
Lift it as fast as possible to save time
A lift plan, and the footpath closed off with barriers

questions.stem: What is an inspection and test plan (ITP)?
options: A list of the times when the inspector takes lunch
A list of the checks, when they happen and who signs them
A test that every trainee must pass to join the team
A plan for when to test the fire alarms during the job and after

questions.stem: The plan marks the fit-up of a staircase as a hold point. What does this mean for the team?
options: They may weld it at once if they are short of time
They take their lunch break at that stage of the job
Work stops there until the fit-up check is signed off
They hold the parts in clamps overnight before they are welded

questions.stem: Why does a planner put the weld inspection into the plan before the painting?
options: Faults hidden under paint are hard to find and fix
Paint will not stick to a weld that is checked
Inspectors are not allowed to look at painted steel at all
So the painters can rest while the inspector works

questions.stem: The plan must state which standard, drawing and revision the job is built to. Why?
options: So everyone works to the same agreed requirements
So the planner can change it later without telling anyone
Because standards always list the price of the job
So the team knows which shop sells the drawing

questions.stem: Who should approve the job plan before the work starts?
options: The newest trainee, so that they learn the plan
Nobody, as long as the team leader wrote it
The supervisor, and the customer where the scope is involved
The material supplier, who knows the steel best

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a pre-start briefing on the first day of a job?
options: To share out the lunch money for the week ahead
To let the customer meet each member of the team
To share the plan, roles and hazards
To decide which team members can go home early

questions.stem: Why should the plan say who to contact for each kind of problem, such as materials, safety or design?
options: So that every problem goes straight to the customer
So that the team leader never has to answer any calls
So problems are kept quiet until the job ends
So the right person is told and can decide quickly

questions.stem: Halfway through a 10-day job, the team has finished 40% of the work. If the work was planned to go at an even rate, what does this show?
options: The job is ahead of the plan by about 10%
The job is exactly on the plan
The job is behind the plan by about 10%
Nothing until the job is finished

questions.stem: The plasma cutter breaks down on day 2 of a 6-day job. What should the team leader do?
options: Stop the whole job until the cutter is repaired
Tell no one and hope the cutter starts again
Use the grinder to cut all the plate freehand
Report it, switch to the back-up method and update the plan

questions.stem: What is a variation (change) order?
options: A note that the team has changed its lunch time
A list of the colours of paint the customer may choose
A notice that the supplier has changed the price
A written, agreed change to the scope, cost or time

questions.stem: Why must every change to the job be written down and agreed, even a small one?
options: To avoid disputes about what was asked for and the cost
Because small changes are always free to the customer
So that the team can blame the customer if it goes wrong
Because spoken words are not allowed on a job site

questions.stem: What is the best way to record daily progress on a site job?
options: Remember it all and tell the supervisor at the end
A dated diary or log, filled in daily
Photos on a personal phone, kept private
A note on the back of the delivery slip

questions.stem: What should the handover of a finished job to the customer include?
options: Only the bill, as the customer can see the work
A walk-round check, the records and care advice
The team's opinion of the customer's taste
A promise that the work will never need any maintenance

questions.stem: At the job review, the team finds that the welding took 30% longer than planned. What is the most useful action?
options: Ignore it, as the job is now finished
Find the cause and adjust future estimates
Blame the welders and cut their hours
Plan the next job with double the time for everything

questions.stem: Which records should be kept on file after a fabrication job is closed out?
options: Only the receipt for the paint and the gas
Drawings, inspection records, changes and handover
The team's lunch orders and the radio station list
Nothing at all, once the customer has paid in full

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the bar chart, named after the engineer who made it popular, that shows each task of a job against a timeline?
A job needs 120 welder-hours. Four welders each work 7.5 hours a day. How many working days are needed?

Task A (2 days), then Task B (4 days), then Task C (3 days) are done one after another. Task D (5 days) runs at the same time as A and B, and must finish before C starts. How many days does the whole job take?
What is the term for the time between ordering an item and it arriving?
Materials for a job cost J$80 000. The planner adds 15% for contingency. What is the total allowance for materials, in J$?
What is the name of the list of small faults that must be put right before a job is handed over?
What is the name of a drawing that has been updated to show the work exactly as it was built?
What is the name for the first agreed version of a schedule, which progress is measured against?
A job has 24 window grills to make, and 15 are finished. What percentage of the grills is complete?
A job was estimated at 60 hours of work but took 72 hours. By what percentage did it overrun the estimate?
A job starts on Monday 2 March and needs 8 working days, Monday to Friday only. On which day of the week does it finish?
What is the name for the first item made in a batch, which is checked before the rest are made?
A crane costs J$45 000 a day to hire, with a minimum hire of 2 days. The lift takes 1 day. What is the hire cost, in J$?
What is the name of the formal written question sent to the designer or client when a drawing is unclear? Give its name or its letters.
One plate, 2.4 m × 1.2 m, gives 8 brackets. How many whole plates are needed to make 60 brackets?

essays.stem: A hotel in Negril asks your team to make and fit 30 m of stainless steel balcony railing. Explain how you would define the scope and gather all the information you need before you plan the job.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would meet the client and agree the scope in writing: the length and design of the railing, the grade and finish of the stainless steel, the fixing method, the completion date, and what is not included, such as repairs to the concrete or tiling. I would visit the site to measure each balcony, check the fixing points and the condition of the concrete, and note access, power, parking, working hours and any guests or staff nearby. I would get the drawings, the specification and any standard the railing must meet, such as the height and the gap between bars, and check that they agree with each other; any difference goes back to the client as a written query. I would find out the hotel's rules for hot work and permits. Then I would check what materials, fixings, tools and skills are needed and whether we have them, and record all of this in a scope statement that the client and the supervisor sign before planning goes on.
markingPoints: Agrees the scope in writing with the client, including what is excluded
Site visit: measures, checks fixing points, access, power, working hours and people nearby
Gets drawings, specification and standard requirements and checks they agree; raises written queries
Finds out the site's permit and hot work rules
Records a scope statement signed by the client and supervisor

essays.stem: A job has these tasks: A cut parts (2 days); B weld frames (4 days, after A); C make brackets (1 day, after A); D galvanise (3 days, after B and C); E prepare site (2 days, any time before F); F install (2 days, after D and E). Find the critical path, the job length and the float on C and E, and explain what these mean.
essays.modelAnswer: The critical path is the longest chain of linked tasks through the job, and it sets the shortest time in which the whole job can be finished. Here, A takes days 1 to 2. B follows and takes days 3 to 6. C can run at the same time as B, on day 3. D must wait for both B and C, so it takes days 7 to 9. F must wait for D, so it takes days 10 to 11. The critical path is A, B, D, F, and the job takes 2 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 11 days. Float is how long a task can slip without delaying the finish. C takes 1 day but B takes 4, so C has 3 days of float. E only has to be finished by the end of day 9, before F starts. It could be done on days 1 to 2, so it has 7 days of float. Any delay to A, B, D or F delays the whole job, so those tasks are watched most closely.
markingPoints: Explains the critical path as the longest chain that sets the finish time
Identifies the critical path A, B, D, F
Job length 11 days, with working
Float on C is 3 days and on E is 7 days, with working
Explains float and that delays on critical tasks delay the whole job

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan the labour, equipment and materials for a job so that each is ready when it is needed, and what you would do if two tasks need the same resource at the same time.
essays.modelAnswer: From the task list and schedule I would work out what each task needs: the number of people and their skills or qualifications, the machines and tools, and the materials with their quantities. For labour, I would check who is free and qualified on each day, allowing for leave and other jobs. For equipment, I would book the machines, cranes or hired items for the right days and check that they will be serviced and working. For materials, I would make the cut list and order list, check the lead times, and order early enough, with delivery dates written into the schedule and a check on arrival. If two tasks need the same welder or machine at the same time, I would first use the float on the non-critical task to move it. If that is not enough, I would look at sharing shifts, using another qualified person or a second machine, or hiring, and weigh the cost against the delay. I would update the plan and tell everyone affected.
markingPoints: Works out labour, skills, equipment and materials for each task from the schedule
Checks availability of people and qualifications; books and checks equipment
Orders materials in time using lead times; delivery dates in the schedule; checks on arrival
Clash: uses float on the non-critical task first
Other options (shifts, another person or machine, hire) weighed against cost; plan updated and shared

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare a time and cost estimate for a fabrication job, including labour, materials, equipment, contingency and GCT. Use a short worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: Start from the task list. For each task, estimate the hours, using records from similar jobs, and add them up. Multiply the hours by the labour rate: for example 40 hours at J$1 500 an hour is J$60 000. From the cut list and the fittings list, price the materials from current supplier quotes, allowing for waste: say J$85 000. Add equipment and consumables, such as gas, discs and a hired scissor lift: say J$15 000. This gives a direct cost of J$160 000. Add the company's overheads and profit as its rules say. Then add a contingency for risks such as rain or late delivery, for example 10% of J$160 000, which is J$16 000, giving J$176 000 before tax. GCT is then added at the current rate, shown as a separate line. The time estimate comes from the schedule, with some float for risks. Write down the assumptions, such as access and working hours, so that the estimate can be checked and changed if the job changes.
markingPoints: Labour: hours from the task list and past records, times the rate (worked figure)
Materials from the cut list with waste, priced from current quotes
Equipment, hire and consumables included; overheads and profit as the company's rules say
Contingency worked out correctly (for example 10%)
GCT at the current rate shown separately; time from the schedule; assumptions written down

essays.stem: Your team will cut and weld a new steel support frame inside a working hotel kitchen in Ocho Rios. Explain the risks you would plan for, and the permits and controls you would put in the plan.
essays.modelAnswer: The main risks are fire from sparks and spatter near grease, gas lines and stores; fume and smoke in a closed room, which can also set off the fire alarm; electric shock from welding near wet floors; burns to staff and guests; noise; trips from cables and hoses; and contamination of food. I would plan the work with the hotel's manager and safety officer, at a time when the kitchen is closed, and get a hot work permit, which sets the controls. The plan would include: clearing or covering anything that can burn for at least 10 m, closing off the area with screens and signs, isolating the kitchen gas where needed, removing or covering food and equipment, local fume extraction and ventilation, and agreeing with the hotel how the smoke detectors are handled. Welding leads and tools must be checked, and floors kept dry. A fire watch with an extinguisher stays during the work and for the time the permit says after it. The emergency contacts and first aid are written in the plan.
markingPoints: Names the main risks: fire, fume, shock, burns, trips, food contamination
Plans with the hotel and works when the kitchen is closed
Hot work permit; combustibles cleared or covered; area screened and signed; gas isolated where needed
Fume extraction and ventilation; smoke detectors agreed with the hotel; equipment checked and floors dry
Fire watch during and after; emergency contacts and first aid in the plan

essays.stem: Explain what an inspection and test plan (ITP) is, and describe what it should contain for a welded steel staircase.
essays.modelAnswer: An inspection and test plan lists every check that will be made on a job, in the order of the work, with what is checked, how it is checked, what it must meet, who does it and the record that proves it. It also marks hold points, where work must stop until the check is signed off, and witness points, where the client may come to watch. For a welded staircase it would include: checking the drawings and revision; checking the material certificates and sizes on delivery; checking that the welders are qualified for the procedure; checking the cut parts and the fit-up of the stringers, treads and landing against the drawing before welding, as a hold point; visual inspection of every weld for size and defects, and any other tests the specification asks for; checking the overall sizes, levels and rise and going of the steps; checking the surface preparation and the paint or galvanising thickness; and a final inspection at handover. Each line gives the record to be kept, such as an inspection sheet or photo.
markingPoints: Defines an ITP: each check, how, acceptance criteria, who, and the record
Explains hold points and witness points
Staircase: drawings, material certificates and welder qualifications checked
Staircase: fit-up before welding, weld inspection, sizes, levels and steps checked
Staircase: coating checks and final inspection, with records for each line

essays.stem: Explain how you would present a job plan to the supervisor, the customer and your team, and why each of them needs different information.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor needs the full plan, because he or she approves it and answers for the cost, safety and quality. I would go through the scope, schedule, resources, estimate, risk assessment, permits and inspection plan, and ask for approval or changes. The customer mainly needs to know what will be done and what will not, the dates, the price, any access or disruption at the site, and what the customer must provide, such as power or a clear area. I would explain it in plain words, with the drawing and a simple timeline, and get the customer's written agreement. The team needs to know what to do and how to do it safely: the tasks and who does each one, the order of work and the dates, the hazards and controls, the permits, the hold points and quality checks, and who to go to with a problem. I would brief them at a pre-start meeting, check that they understand by asking questions, and give out the job sheets.
markingPoints: Supervisor: full plan for approval (scope, schedule, cost, risk, quality)
Customer: scope, exclusions, dates, price, disruption and what they must provide
Customer: plain words and written agreement
Team: tasks and roles, sequence, hazards and controls, permits, hold points, contacts
Briefs the team, checks understanding, gives out job sheets

essays.stem: Describe how you would monitor progress against the plan on a two-week job, and how you would deal with a request from the customer to change the design part-way through.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set a baseline schedule and check progress each day, by walking the job, counting finished items and asking the team. I would record progress in a site diary and mark it on the schedule, compare the work done and the hours and materials used with the plan, and look ahead to the next few days for problems such as deliveries or permits. Each week I would report the progress, any delays and the forecast finish date to the supervisor. If a task on the critical path slips, I act at once, for example by moving resources or using float. If the customer asks to change the design, I would not start the change straight away. I would write down exactly what is wanted, then work out the effect on cost, time, materials, safety and any work already done. I would put this to the supervisor and the customer as a variation, and only go ahead when it is agreed in writing. Then I would update the drawings, the plan and the schedule and brief the team.
markingPoints: Baseline set; progress checked daily and recorded in a diary and on the schedule
Compares work done, hours and materials with the plan; looks ahead for problems
Reports progress and forecast to the supervisor; acts quickly on critical delays
Change: writes it down and works out the effect on cost, time, materials and safety
Proceeds only on a written, agreed variation; updates drawings, plan and team

essays.stem: Explain how you would build contingency into the plan for a site job in the rainy season, giving examples of risks and the backup plans you would make.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would list the risks that could delay or harm the job, judge how likely and how serious each is, and plan a response for the main ones. In the rainy season, rain can stop welding and painting outdoors, make access roads muddy and make electrical work unsafe. Backup plans would include doing as much fabrication and painting as possible in the workshop, so that only fitting is done on site; having tarpaulins or a temporary shelter; and planning indoor work for wet days. Late delivery of steel is another risk, so I would order early, check stock, and name a second supplier. A machine breakdown could be covered by a spare machine or a hire company booked in advance. Sickness could be covered by a trained person from another team. I would add some spare time to the schedule and a contingency sum to the estimate, and agree with the supervisor who may use them. The plan would also say when the backup plans are triggered.
markingPoints: Lists risks and judges likelihood and seriousness
Weather: prefabricate in the workshop, shelter, indoor work on wet days; electrical safety
Materials: order early, second supplier
Equipment and people: spare or hired machine, trained cover
Spare time and a contingency sum in the plan, with triggers and who may use them

essays.stem: Describe how you would close out a complete activity: the final checks, the handover, the records and a review. Explain how the review improves future plans.
essays.modelAnswer: Before handover I would carry out a final inspection against the drawing, the specification and the inspection plan, and make a snag list of anything to put right. When the snags are cleared, the area is cleaned and the waste, offcuts and equipment are removed. I would walk round the work with the customer, show that it meets what was agreed, hand over the records, such as inspection sheets, material certificates and care advice for the paint or galvanising, and get the handover signed. I would update the drawings to as-built if anything changed. Then I would file the plan, the changes, the records and the costs. Finally I would hold a short review with the team and the supervisor: compare the planned and actual time, cost and materials, list what went well and what went wrong, and find the causes. The lessons are written down and used to improve the estimates, the checklists and the methods on the next job, so that future plans are more accurate and safer.
markingPoints: Final inspection against drawing and specification; snag list cleared
Site cleaned; equipment and waste removed
Handover walk-round with the customer; records handed over and signed; as-built drawings
Plans, changes, records and costs filed
Review compares planned and actual, finds causes, and the lessons improve future plans

practical1.title: Prepare and present a complete job plan for a fabrication contract
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the team a job brief and a drawing, for example: make and install six window grills and a pedestrian gate for a community centre in Old Harbour, painted, to be finished in three weeks. As a team, prepare a complete plan for the job: (1) a scope statement with what is and is not included, and a list of any questions to the client; (2) a work breakdown and a sequence of tasks; (3) a cut list and materials order with a waste allowance; (4) a bar chart (Gantt chart) that shows the critical path, the float and the milestones; (5) a labour and equipment schedule; (6) a cost estimate with labour, materials, equipment and a contingency, with GCT at the rate the assessor gives; (7) a risk assessment with the permits needed; and (8) an inspection and test plan with hold points. Each member prepares at least one part, and another member checks it. The team then presents the plan to the assessor, acting as supervisor and client, in a 15-minute briefing in which every member speaks. Photograph each document and each stage of the briefing and add them to the group's practical.
materials: Job brief and drawing from the assessor
Planning forms: scope statement, cut list, order list, risk assessment and inspection and test plan
Large chart paper or a whiteboard for the bar chart
Supplier price list and labour rates from the assessor
The Centre's computer with a spreadsheet, if available
photos: The scope statement and the list of questions for the client
The work breakdown and the cut list with the materials order
The bar chart showing the critical path, float and milestones
The cost estimate, with contingency and GCT shown separately
The risk assessment and the inspection and test plan with hold points
The team presenting the plan, with each member speaking
The assessor's questions and the team's notes of the changes agreed
checklist: Prepared their part of the plan accurately and completely
Checked another member's part and corrected any errors
Calculations (quantities, waste, hours, costs) are correct
The bar chart shows a sensible sequence with the correct critical path and float
Risk assessment names real hazards, sensible controls and the permits needed
Inspection and test plan has clear checks, acceptance criteria and hold points
Explained their part clearly in the briefing and answered questions
Worked well with the team and met the time allowed
safety: This is a planning task: keep the planning room tidy and walkways clear
If the team visits the workshop or yard to check materials, wear safety boots and follow the Centre's rules
Do not lift or move stock during the task without the assessor's permission
Use the Centre's computer and accounts only as the Centre allows

practical2.title: Plan, carry out and review a small fabrication activity: two steel trestles
practical2.brief: As a team, plan, make and review two matching steel trestles (sawhorses) from the drawing the assessor gives you. First write a one-page plan: the task list and sequence, the time for each task, who does what, the cut list with a waste allowance, the hazards and controls, and the hold points. Put the plan on a wall chart. Then carry out the job. Every 30 minutes the team leader marks progress on the chart, and the team agrees what to do about any delay. The fit-up of the first trestle is a hold point: the assessor must sign it off before welding. Every member cuts, fits or welds at least one part while the assessor watches, and the team leader role changes half way. When the trestles are finished, check them against the drawing and record the results. Hand them over to the assessor with the records. Finally hold a 15-minute review: compare the planned and actual times and materials, list what went well and what to change, and write it down. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and records to the group's practical.
materials: Drawing of the trestle from the assessor
Steel square tube or angle (for example 40 × 40 × 3 mm), enough for two trestles plus a waste allowance
Cut-off saw or bandsaw, angle grinder, and a welding set (MIG or MMAW) with consumables
Tape, square, scriber, clamps and a welding table
Plan sheet, wall chart, inspection sheet and review sheet
photos: The written plan and the wall chart before work starts
Parts cut and labelled, laid out against the cut list
The first trestle tacked, with the assessor's hold point sign-off
The wall chart part-way through, showing progress and any changes
Both finished trestles side by side, with a tape across the key sizes
The completed inspection sheet and the review notes
checklist: Took part in writing the plan and can explain the sequence and timings
Carried out their task to the plan, safely and to the drawing
Kept to the hold point and did not weld before sign-off
Tracked progress and helped decide what to do about delays
Led, or followed the leader's instructions, and communicated clearly
Finished trestles within the tolerance given (for example ±2 mm on the key sizes)
Gave useful points in the review, comparing planned and actual
safety: Wear full PPE for cutting, grinding and welding, with eye protection when grinding
Weld only in a booth or behind screens; warn others before striking an arc
Clamp work before cutting; keep hands clear of saw blades
Remove anything that can burn and keep an extinguisher at hand
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
